bug_description.normalized: The staged 230-byte witness targets the `-DSYNTAX_TEST` Oniguruma harness. Its 8-byte control header `de 5d 72 88 3f 3f 9c f3` decodes to `enc = GB18030`, `syntax = PERL_NG`, `options = 0x3f3f8872`, `pattern_size = 156`, and `backward = false`. The compile-time option bits include `ONIG_OPTION_TEXT_SEGMENT_WORD`, but the runtime bits are only `NOT_BEGIN_POSITION | CALLBACK_EACH_MATCH`, so the built-in `CHECK_VALIDITY_OF_STRING` search-time guard is absent. `alloc_exec()` copies the first 156 payload bytes into `pattern`, then runs the same bytes through `fix_size()` and copies only the first 80 bytes into a separate `data_pattern` buffer; the saved ASan allocation context at `harnesses/base.c:437` confirms that this crashing object is exactly 80 bytes long. That 80-byte buffer ends in byte `0xf2`, which is a GB18030 `CM` lead byte, so `data_pattern` is not a valid GB18030 string. The regex bytes include `\X`; under `ONIG_OPTION_TEXT_SEGMENT_WORD`, parsing and code generation turn that into `OP_TEXT_SEGMENT_BOUNDARY` with `type = WORD_BOUNDARY`, so matching reaches `onigenc_wb_is_break_position()`. The vulnerable `exec()` path immediately calls `search(reg, data_pattern, data_pattern_end, options, backward, sl)` on the truncated buffer, whereas the later `str` search is guarded by `onigenc_is_valid_mbc_string()` and the staged patch adds the same missing check around this first search. During the saved crashing run, `onigenc_wb_is_break_position()` decodes the current position `p` with `ONIGENC_MBC_TO_CODE(enc, p, end)`; the ASan report says the invalid read is 0 bytes to the right of the 80-byte `data_pattern` allocation, so on this call `p` is the final byte `0xf2`. `onigenc_mbn_mbc_to_code()` therefore asks `enclen(enc, p)` for the GB18030 character length, `gb18030_mbc_enc_len()` treats `0xf2` as a multibyte lead, increments `p`, and executes `if (GB18030_MAP[*p] == C4)` on the missing second byte one past the heap object, producing the saved `AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1` at `src/gb18030.c:85`.

source.description: Source. First non-entry project statement on the vulnerable path that materializes the exact malformed search buffer: `alloc_exec()` copies the witness prefix into a standalone 80-byte `data_pattern` heap object that is later searched under GB18030.
source.value_from: The staged `gt_results/arvo_53046/poc` witness is 230 bytes with SHA-256 `506dcbb121b318edaf4fac034323cad136551eeb6e2d785027e54ef97512767d`. Its 8-byte `fuzzer_syntax` header selects `GB18030`, `PERL_NG`, `options = 0x3f3f8872`, `pattern_size = 156`, and `backward = false`; `fix_size()` then shrinks the copied `data_pattern` to 80 bytes, whose tail bytes are `53 5d 35 33 3b 35 36 f2`, leaving final byte `0xf2` as an unterminated GB18030 lead byte.

relation.description: Source identity relation for the vulnerability-relevant value.

root_cause.code: r = search(reg, data_pattern, data_pattern_end, options, backward, sl);
root_cause.description: Root cause. `exec()` searches `data_pattern` before any unconditional multibyte-string validation, even though this path can pass a truncated non-owning prefix buffer into GB18030 matching.
root_cause.note: The same function validates the later `str` search at lines 367-370 with `onigenc_is_valid_mbc_string(enc, str, end)`, and the staged patch repairs this exact omission by wrapping the step-7 call in `if (data_pattern == pattern || onigenc_is_valid_mbc_string(enc, data_pattern, data_pattern_end) != 0)`.

sink.description: ASan sink. GB18030 length decoding dereferences the missing second byte of the truncated multibyte character one byte past the `data_pattern` heap object.
sink.note: The saved sanitizer trace reports `READ of size 1` at `src/gb18030.c:85:19`, and says the bad address is 0 bytes to the right of the 80-byte region `[0x607000002e80, 0x607000002ed0)` allocated at `harnesses/base.c:437`.

tainted_value_origin.description: The `fuzzer_syntax` control header interprets the first 8 witness bytes as the execution state that matters for the vulnerability: GB18030 dispatch, PERL_NG parsing, compile/runtime option bits, the 156-byte pattern split, and forward-search mode.
tainted_value_origin.value_from: Header bytes `de 5d 72 88 3f 3f 9c f3` decode to `enc = GB18030`, `syntax = PERL_NG`, `options = 0x3f3f8872`, `pattern_size = 156`, and `backward = false`. The runtime subset lacks `ONIG_OPTION_CHECK_VALIDITY_OF_STRING`.

parser_admitted.code:
r = onig_new(&reg, pattern, pattern_end,
             (options & OPTIONS_AT_COMPILE), enc, syntax, &einfo);
parser_admitted.description: Oniguruma accepts the 156-byte pattern and begins compiling it under the GB18030 / PERL_NG configuration derived from the witness header. The later crash occurs during the first search on `data_pattern`, not during this initial compile admission.

evidence_limitations: The staged patch commit message names OSS-Fuzz issue 49746 rather than 53046, but the diff hunk itself directly wraps the exact step-7 `search(reg, data_pattern, data_pattern_end, ...)` call on this sample's crash path.

No fixed-image run is staged here (`prepare_report.json` says `fix_image_available=false`), so `sanitizer_ground_truth.patch_resolves` remains false even though the patch text clearly adds the missing validity guard.

The staged artifacts do not expose the exact search-loop iteration count that placed `s` on the final byte of `data_pattern`; that position is inferred from the 80-byte allocation size, the copied tail byte `0xf2`, and ASan's report that the invalid read occurred exactly one byte past the right edge.

fine_trace.note: Unscored harness-header decode. The staged `-DSYNTAX_TEST` witness bytes `de 5d 72 88 3f 3f 9c f3` select `enc = GB18030`, `syntax = PERL_NG`, `options = 0x3f3f8872`, `pattern_size = 156`, and `backward = false`. The compile bits include `ONIG_OPTION_TEXT_SEGMENT_WORD`, while the runtime bits are only `NOT_BEGIN_POSITION | CALLBACK_EACH_MATCH`, so the later search will not request `CHECK_VALIDITY_OF_STRING`.

The first 156 payload bytes after the 8-byte header are materialized as the standalone regex `pattern` buffer that `onig_new()` compiles. Those bytes include `\X`, which later expands into text-segment-boundary logic.

Source. The witness pattern bytes are copied again into a separate search buffer after `fix_size()` shrinks them to 80 bytes on the slow-pattern path. The saved ASan allocation context at line 437 identifies this 80-byte heap object as the crashing allocation, and its last copied byte is `0xf2`, a GB18030 `CM` lead byte, so `data_pattern` is not a valid GB18030 string before search begins.

While compiling the regex bytes from step 2, each witness `\X` is rewritten into an internal expression that contains `ANCR_NO_TEXT_SEGMENT_BOUNDARY` (`\Y`) rather than a literal character. That anchor node is the future trigger for the Unicode word-break path.

Because the compile-time options from step 1 have `ONIG_OPTION_TEXT_SEGMENT_WORD` set, the text-segment anchor from step 4 is marked `TEXT_SEGMENT_WORD` instead of the default grapheme-cluster mode. That status bit is the selector used later in code generation.

Code generation emits `OP_TEXT_SEGMENT_BOUNDARY` for the anchor and, because `ND_IS_TEXT_SEGMENT_WORD(node)` is true from step 5, records `type = WORD_BOUNDARY`. This is the exact opcode path that later reaches `onigenc_wb_is_break_position()` from `match_at()`.

fine_trace.code: r = search(reg, data_pattern, data_pattern_end, options, backward, sl);
fine_trace.note: Root cause step. `exec()` searches the truncated `data_pattern` buffer from step 3 before any unconditional multibyte validation. The same function validates the later `str` search with `onigenc_is_valid_mbc_string(enc, str, end)` at lines 367-370, and the staged patch repairs this exact omission by adding a corresponding guard around this first `search()` call.

The optional built-in validity gate exists here, but the runtime option mask from step 1 does not contain `ONIG_OPTION_CHECK_VALIDITY_OF_STRING`. This block is therefore skipped for the step-7 search, and the invalid GB18030 `data_pattern` continues into matching.

When the compiled opcode from step 6 executes during the step-7 search, `match_at()` takes the `TEXT_SEGMENT_BOUNDARY` / `WORD_BOUNDARY` arm and asks the Unicode word-break helper to decode the current candidate position `s` inside `data_pattern`.

fine_trace.code:
cfrom = ONIGENC_MBC_TO_CODE(enc, prev, end);
cto   = ONIGENC_MBC_TO_CODE(enc, p, end);
fine_trace.note: The word-break helper decodes both sides of the candidate boundary. The saved ASan read is 0 bytes to the right of the 80-byte `data_pattern` allocation, and step 3 shows that allocation ends with lead byte `0xf2`, so this `ONIGENC_MBC_TO_CODE(enc, p, end)` call is decoding the final byte of `data_pattern` as a GB18030 character.

Generic multibyte decoding first asks the encoding-specific `enclen(enc, p)` how long the character is, without consulting `end`. For the GB18030 trailing lead byte from step 10, `enclen` dispatches into `gb18030_mbc_enc_len()`.

Sink. `GB18030_MAP[*p] != CM` is false for the final byte `0xf2`, so `gb18030_mbc_enc_len()` increments `p` and immediately reads `GB18030_MAP[*p]` for the missing second byte. Because `p` already pointed at `data_pattern[79]`, this dereference lands exactly one byte past the 80-byte heap object and matches the saved ASan `heap-buffer-overflow READ of size 1` at `src/gb18030.c:85`.

poc.trigger: Run the staged 230-byte witness against the vulnerable `fuzzer` build compiled with `-DSYNTAX_TEST`. Its 8-byte header selects `GB18030`, `PERL_NG`, `options = 0x3f3f8872`, `pattern_size = 156`, and `backward = false`, which makes `alloc_exec()` build an 80-byte `data_pattern` ending in lead byte `0xf2` and then search it without the validity guard later added by the patch.

format.name: Oniguruma fuzzer_syntax witness
format.contract: Exact 230-byte witness whose first 8 bytes are `de 5d 72 88 3f 3f 9c f3`; under the staged `-DSYNTAX_TEST` harness those bytes decode to `GB18030`, `PERL_NG`, `options = 0x3f3f8872`, `pattern_size = 156`, and `backward = false`, and the first 80 bytes of the pattern region end in `0xf2`, leaving `data_pattern` as an invalid GB18030 string when searched.
